rows: JobTracker = resource mgmt + job scheduling in one monolith
ResourceManager (global scheduler) separated from per-job ApplicationMaster
key: Hadoop 1.x's single JobTracker mixed resource management with MapReduce job scheduling (MapReduce only, ~4,000-node ceiling); YARN (Hadoop 2.0, 2013) split this into a global ResourceManager and a per-job ApplicationMaster, so any framework can share a 10,000+ node cluster.
cue: If the question describes a cluster that can only run MapReduce, stalls near 4,000 nodes, or one daemon doing both scheduling and job tracking, the answer is Hadoop 1.x / JobTracker; if Spark, Tez and MapReduce share one cluster, it is YARN.

slides: P1 s10-11; P2 s7, s11; P1 s28 (MCQ Q1 note)
rows: One per cluster, on a dedicated master node
Scheduler (allocates containers; FIFO/Fair/Capacity) + ApplicationsManager (accepts jobs, starts first container for each AM)
Requests containers from RM, tells NM to launch tasks, monitors progress, re-requests for failed tasks, releases containers
Holds the framework-specific logic (MR AM, Spark AM, Tez AM, Samza AM)
YARN 2.4+: ZooKeeper Active/Standby RM, failover < 60 s
RM restarts the AM (max attempts, default 2)
Spark AM requests 100 containers (4 cores, 8 GB each)
key: The ResourceManager is the single global scheduler that hands out containers for the whole cluster, while an ApplicationMaster is a per-job process that negotiates containers from the RM and runs that one job's tasks.
cue: If the question says 'one per cluster / decides which application gets which containers', the answer is the ResourceManager; if it says 'one per job / requests containers on behalf of the job / restarts failed tasks', it is the ApplicationMaster.

rows: All containers on that node marked failed
AM is notified and re-requests containers elsewhere
New AM recovers state from HDFS checkpoints if the framework supports it (MapReduce: yes; early Spark: no)
YARN 2.4+: ZooKeeper promotes Standby RM in < 60 s
key: A NodeManager failure is caught by the RM through missed heartbeats and the job's AM re-requests the lost containers elsewhere, whereas an AM failure is handled by the RM restarting the AM itself (default 2 attempts), recovering state from HDFS checkpoints if supported.
cue: If the question traces a worker node (e.g. NM2 with 5 containers) dying mid-job, the answer is the NodeManager-failure path (heartbeat timeout -> containers failed -> AM re-requests); if the job's coordinator dies, it is the AM-restart path.

rows: Cluster divided into queues with guaranteed capacity; elastically borrows unused capacity
All jobs get equal share of resources
Engineering 60% / Finance 40%; a2i queues 60/30/10; LinkedIn 6 queues (production 40%)
Latency-sensitive short jobs complete quickly even if a large job is running
SLAs: production queue guaranteed minimum; adhoc queries cannot starve revenue pipelines
FIFO: one queue, submission order; one long job starves all others
FIFO not suitable for multi-tenant clusters
key: The Capacity Scheduler gives each team's queue a guaranteed percentage of the cluster (lending idle capacity), whereas the Fair Scheduler shares resources equally among running jobs so short jobs finish fast; FIFO simply runs jobs in submission order and lets one long job starve the rest.
cue: If the question describes several teams/departments that each need a guaranteed share (e.g. 60% health batch, 30% streaming, 10% ad hoc), the answer is the Capacity Scheduler; if many short interactive jobs must not wait behind a big one, it is the Fair Scheduler; a single queue in arrival order is FIFO.

rows: Record by record (id, name, age, score together)
Parquet reads ~300 GB (33x speedup; 97% I/O reduction)
Min/max stats per row group -> predicate pushdown skips row groups
Portability, small data; row-append streaming ingest (Avro)
Analytical, read-heavy workloads (Spark, Presto, ML, Hive)
key: A row store keeps each record's fields together so any query reads every column, while a columnar store keeps each column together so a query reads only the columns it needs (3 of 100 columns -> ~3% of the data).
cue: If the question describes an analyst query that touches a few columns of a very wide table and is slow on CSV, the answer is to switch to columnar (Parquet/ORC); if it describes appending whole events or exchanging records, a row format (Avro/CSV) fits.

rows: Schema evolution: missing fields use defaults, extra fields ignored (backward + forward compatible)
Row groups (~128 MB) with min/max stats -> predicate pushdown
Streaming ingest Kafka -> HDFS; data exchange
key: Avro is a row-oriented format whose reader/writer schema handles schema evolution, so it suits append-heavy streaming ingest, whereas Parquet is columnar with per-row-group statistics, so it suits analytic reads that select few columns and filter.
cue: If the question describes LinkedIn adding a new field to Kafka events without breaking old consumers, the answer is Avro; if it describes analysts running Spark/Presto queries over a few columns, it is Parquet.

slides: P1 s17, s25, s28 (MCQ Q2 note), s30 (T/F 4); W07 P2 s12
rows: Spark, Presto, ML pipelines (broader standard for analytics)
Predicate pushdown via row-group stats; Spark-native
Hive ACID support; vectorized reads; pushdown within stripes
Developed by the Hive team (2013); 2-4x faster reads than SequenceFile
key: Both are columnar, but ORC is optimised for Hive (best compression, Hive ACID, vectorized reads) while Parquet is the broader analytics standard across Spark, Presto and ML.
cue: If the question describes a Hive SQL warehouse needing ACID and maximum compression, the answer is ORC (+Zlib); if it describes a Spark/Presto/ML pipeline, it is Parquet (+Snappy).

rows: HDFS can start reading from any point in the file without decompressing from the beginning
Multiple Mappers process different parts simultaneously (e.g. 3 row groups -> 3 Mappers)
Parquet splits at row-group boundaries; bzip2 natively splittable
MapReduce cannot split across gzip boundaries even though HDFS stores it in blocks
Best practice: Parquet + Snappy for analytics
'The Gzip Trap - very common mistake'; avoid raw gzip on large CSV
key: A splittable file can be read from any point so many Mappers work on it in parallel, whereas a gzip-compressed CSV must be decompressed from the start, so one Mapper reads the whole file.
cue: If the question describes a big gzip CSV processed by a single slow Mapper (e.g. telecom CDRs taking 6 hours), the answer is 'not splittable - convert to Parquet+Snappy (or bzip2)'.

rows: LZO: fast/medium, splittable with index; Zstd: fast/high, block-level
Bzip2: slowest/highest, splittable; ORC + Zlib for Hive warehouse
key: Snappy trades a medium compression ratio for high speed, whereas Gzip compresses more but slowly; neither is splittable on raw files, so both are used inside splittable containers like Parquet.
cue: If the question asks for a codec for a speed-critical Spark analytics or Kafka ingest pipeline, the answer is Snappy; for storage-heavy ML feature files it lists Gzip; for cold archive, Zstd; if splittability on a raw file is required, bzip2 or LZO+index.

rows: Cluster A MapReduce/Hive ETL, B experimental Spark, C Samza
One 5,000-node YARN cluster, Capacity Scheduler with 6 queues
Three configurations tripled ops cost; cross-cluster data movement added latency
One cluster, fair sharing + framework isolation
key: Running each framework on its own cluster left each under-used (45%), whereas consolidating them onto one YARN cluster with Capacity queues raised utilisation to 78% and served 73% more work on the same hardware.
cue: If the question describes a company running separate MapReduce, Spark and streaming clusters that sit idle at different times, the answer is to consolidate onto one YARN cluster with Capacity Scheduler queues.

rows: 2013; cluster OS for EMR, HDInsight, CDP through 2020
2018-present; largely replaced YARN for new deployments
Global scheduler / node agent / per-app master
Pod (YARN container is its direct ancestor)
Spark on YARN in on-premise Hadoop clusters
key: Kubernetes has largely replaced YARN for new deployments, but it keeps YARN's three-tier design, and its Pod descends directly from YARN's container.
cue: If the question asks what replaced YARN, or where the container idea went, the answer is Kubernetes (Pods); if it is about an on-premise Hadoop cluster running Spark, it is still YARN.

rows: Slow (disk per iteration); K-Means 100 iters = 10 TB I/O
map, filter, join, groupBy, SQL, ML, stream; Python, Scala, Java, R
Not supported natively; not feasible (>30 s)
Single-pass batch where Spark's ~8 GB/Executor overhead is prohibitive, or stable MR code
ML, graph, interactive, streaming, >2 iterations over same data
key: MapReduce writes every intermediate result to HDFS, so iterative jobs pay disk I/O on every pass, whereas Spark caches the working set in memory as RDDs and recovers from lineage, making iterative work 10-100x faster.
cue: If the question describes an ML or graph job that loops many times over the same data (K-Means, logistic regression, PageRank), the answer is Spark; a one-pass batch job on a huge cluster with tight memory can stay on MapReduce.

rows: JVM processes launched on Worker Nodes
Builds the DAG of transformations; coordinates execution; schedules tasks
Receives tasks scheduled by the Driver
Stores cached RDD partitions in memory
Cluster Manager allocates resources: YARN, Kubernetes, Mesos, Standalone
key: The Driver runs main() and turns the program into a DAG of tasks and schedules them, while Executors are JVM processes on worker nodes that actually run those tasks and hold cached partitions.
cue: If the question asks which component builds the DAG or where collect() results land, the answer is the Driver; where tasks run and cached RDD partitions live, it is the Executor.

rows: Unifies SQL, DataFrames and RDDs under one entry point
key: SparkContext was the Spark 1.x entry point for RDDs, while SparkSession (2.x+) is the unified entry point for SQL, DataFrames and RDDs, still exposing the context as spark.sparkContext.
cue: If the code starts with SparkSession.builder and uses spark.sql, it is the 2.x+ unified entry point; if it calls sc.textFile on raw RDDs, it uses SparkContext.

rows: Re-read the HDFS input for that partition and re-apply the same transformations
No data replication overhead - 'the computation is the backup'
Expensive for wide dependencies (many ancestors); checkpoint long chains to HDFS
Recomputing from lineage is cheaper than maintaining 3x replicated in-memory state
key: HDFS tolerates failures by storing three copies of the data, whereas an RDD stores only how it was derived and recomputes a lost partition from its parents, so there is no replication overhead.
cue: If the question asks how Spark recovers a lost partition without copying data (e.g. an executor holding partitions 3 and 7 crashes), the answer is lineage recomputation; for HDFS block loss, it is replication.

rows: Lazy: builds the DAG, does not execute
Eager: triggers execution of the DAG
A value to the Driver, or writes to storage
map, filter, flatMap, distinct, reduceByKey, join, groupByKey, cache
collect, count, first, take(n), reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach
No transformation executes until an action is called
Spark then analyses the full DAG, pipelines, runs only needed partitions
key: A transformation lazily defines a new RDD and only adds to the DAG, while an action forces the DAG to run and returns a value to the Driver or writes output.
cue: If the question shows a chain like filter().map() and asks why nothing ran, the answer is that these are lazy transformations; the first count()/collect()/saveAsTextFile() is the action that triggers the job.

rows: Each output partition depends on at most one input partition (1-to-1)
Each output partition may depend on multiple input partitions (all-to-all)
map, filter, flatMap, union, mapPartitions, coalesce
groupByKey, reduceByKey, aggregateByKey, join (not co-partitioned), repartition, distinct, sortByKey
Recompute only that partition from its single parent
Must recompute from all parent partitions (expensive)
key: In a narrow dependency each child partition needs at most one parent partition, so it pipelines in one stage with no shuffle, whereas a wide dependency needs many parent partitions, forcing a network shuffle and a new stage.
cue: If the question shows a DAG and asks where the stage boundary is, put it at the first wide operation (reduceByKey, groupByKey, join, repartition); map/filter chains stay in one stage.

slides: P1 s22; P2 s18 (live exercise Q3)
rows: Applies a local combine (like a MapReduce Combiner)
Avoid when an aggregate is all you need (inference from 'prefer reduceByKey')
Spark UI (localhost:4040) shuffle read/write bytes - smaller
key: Both shuffle, but reduceByKey pre-aggregates values on each partition before the shuffle (like a Combiner), so far less data crosses the network than with groupByKey.
cue: If the question describes a word count or per-key sum that is slow because of heavy shuffle, the answer is to replace groupByKey with reduceByKey.

rows: Recompute only from the single parent partition
key: coalesce reduces the number of partitions without a shuffle (narrow), while repartition reshuffles data across the network (wide) and starts a new stage.
cue: If the question asks for the cheap way to cut partitions before writing output, the answer is coalesce; if it needs a full redistribution, repartition (with a shuffle).

rows: Distributed collection organised into named columns with a schema
Catalyst (predicate pushdown, join reordering, constant folding)
Built on top of RDDs; compiles down to an RDD plan
RDDs largely replaced by DataFrames/Datasets since Spark 2.0
key: A DataFrame adds named columns and a schema so the Catalyst optimiser can rewrite the query before running it (10-100x faster on structured data), whereas an RDD is schema-less records processed with functional operators.
cue: If the question describes structured tabular data queried with SQL/aggregations, the answer is DataFrame/Spark SQL; if it needs custom low-level per-record control, RDD.

rows: Written to local disk, read back
MEMORY_ONLY_SER: Kryo-serialised bytes, smaller but slower; OFF_HEAP: native memory, avoids GC
Reused in >1 action (iterative ML, interactive queries)
Caching single-use RDDs wastes RAM and triggers LRU eviction
LR: Spark MEMORY_ONLY 0.96 s/iter vs Hadoop 127 s/iter (132x)
key: MEMORY_ONLY keeps partitions in the JVM heap and recomputes any that do not fit, whereas MEMORY_AND_DISK spills those partitions to local disk instead of recomputing them.
cue: If the question says the cached dataset is bigger than cluster RAM and recomputation is expensive, the answer is MEMORY_AND_DISK; if it fits in RAM and speed is everything, MEMORY_ONLY.

rows: Samples key distribution, assigns key ranges to partitions
Uniform for random keys; can hot-spot on skewed data
Each partition holds a key range (inference: keeps sort order)
Custom partitioner: co-partition two RDDs on the same key to eliminate shuffle on join
key: A hash partitioner spreads keys by hashCode modulo the partition count (the default, but it can hot-spot on skewed keys), while a range partitioner samples keys and assigns ordered ranges, which sortByKey needs.
cue: If the question involves sorting by key, the answer is the range partitioner; for ordinary key grouping the default hash partitioner; for joining two RDDs without a shuffle, a custom co-partitioner.

rows: Writes sorted runs to disk once, then merges
Spills, merges and re-reads multiple times (twice per byte)
100 TB in 23 min on 206 EC2 nodes (Nov 2013)
All 8 SSDs as shuffle dirs; off-heap sort buffers (Unsafe); single wide sortByKey
3.1x faster (72 -> 23 min); 206 vs 2,100 nodes (P2 s2 says '3x faster on 3.5x fewer machines' - decks differ)
key: Spark won GraySort mainly through a sort-based shuffle that writes sorted runs once and merges them, whereas MapReduce's shuffle spills and re-reads data several times, costing ~200 TB of extra disk I/O at 100 TB.
cue: If the question asks why Spark sorted 100 TB in 23 minutes on 206 nodes versus Hadoop's 72 minutes on 2,100, the answer is sort-based shuffle on SSDs plus off-heap buffers and fewer stages, not just caching.

rows: Smaller (2-5x) when data is larger than RAM
K-Means, logistic regression, graph BFS, interactive queries on the same table
Single-pass batch jobs on very large clusters
Working set cached in RAM and reused; MapReduce cannot cache across jobs
Each byte read once - nothing to reuse
MapReduce acceptable where Spark's ~8 GB/Executor overhead is prohibitive
key: Spark's in-memory caching pays off only when the same working set is reused across iterations (10-100x), while for single-pass ETL over data larger than RAM the gain is small (2-5x) - 'a multiplier, not a panacea'.
cue: If the question asks under what conditions Spark would NOT outperform MapReduce, the answer is a single-pass job over data larger than cluster RAM (or tight memory), not an iterative one.

rows: Spark: Cluster Computing with Working Sets
Resilient Distributed Datasets: A Fault-Tolerant Abstraction for In-Memory Cluster Computing
USENIX NSDI, Rank A*; Best Paper Award
Working set reused across parallel operations; MapReduce cannot cache it
Lineage-based fault tolerance; narrow vs wide dependencies; persistence levels
key: The 2010 HotCloud paper was a short proof-of-concept arguing for caching a reusable working set in memory, while the 2012 NSDI paper formalised RDDs with lineage-based fault tolerance and won Best Paper.
cue: If the question asks which paper introduced lineage-based fault tolerance formally, the answer is NSDI 2012; the 'working set' motivation is HotCloud 2010.

rows: Rejected immediately (INSERT fails if amount is text)
Stored; NULL returned at query ('abc' in amount -> NULL)
Fast write (raw file copy); slower query (parse per query)
Open: ORC, Parquet, CSV, JSON, Avro
key: Schema-on-write validates data against the table schema when it is loaded and rejects bad rows, while schema-on-read stores raw files as-is and applies the schema only when queried, so bad values silently become NULL.
cue: If the question describes loading raw web logs immediately and defining several tables over them later, or a corrupt column quietly returning NULL, the answer is schema-on-read; if an INSERT is rejected for a type error, it is schema-on-write.

gh.note: Schema on write vs on read is the first row of the lecturer's “important exam topics” table.

rows: Limited: only ORC tables in ACID (transactional) mode
Single-node or MPP; database storage engine
key: HiveQL looks like SQL but compiles to distributed batch jobs over HDFS, so it scales to petabytes yet has minute-level latency, limited ACID/UPDATE and no traditional indexes, unlike an RDBMS's millisecond OLTP SQL.
cue: If the question expects millisecond response or row-level UPDATEs from Hive, the answer is the misconception 'HiveQL = SQL'; a COUNT(*) on 1 TB can take 5-10 minutes - use Presto or Spark SQL for interactive latency.

gh.note: The lecturer's course plan lists this table (schema, ACID, UPDATE/DELETE, indexes vs partitions + buckets, latency) as “important exam topics”.

rows: Separate HDFS sub-directory per column value (year=2024/month=01/)
Fixed number of files (buckets) inside each partition
Partition pruning: skips non-matching directories, avoids full-table scan
Bucket map join: bucket i x bucket i, no full sort-merge shuffle
Low-cardinality, used in WHERE (date, country, region, status)
The join key, e.g. user_id (slide example; 'high-cardinality' is general knowledge)
High-cardinality key -> partition explosion (100 M directories crash NameNode)
Both tables must use same key and same bucket count
key: Partitioning splits a table into directories by a low-cardinality column value so WHERE filters skip whole directories, while bucketing hashes a (high-cardinality) column into a fixed number of files so tables bucketed the same way can be joined bucket-to-bucket without a full shuffle.
cue: If the question describes daily reports filtered by country and date, the answer is partition on (country/date); if it describes repeatedly joining with a 10 M-row user table on user_id, bucket on user_id - often both together.

rows: Written in the statement: PARTITION (year=2024, month=1)
Inferred from the last SELECT columns: PARTITION (year, month)
Partition columns must be last in SELECT, in order; otherwise Hive silently assigns values incorrectly
key: A static insert names the exact partition value in the INSERT, while a dynamic insert lets Hive take partition values from the last SELECT columns so many partitions load in one statement.
cue: If the question needs to load 36 months of raw sales into a partitioned table in one statement, the answer is dynamic partition insert (with nonstrict mode and partition columns last).

slides: P1 s6, s17, s26; P1 s29 (MCQ Q4 note); P2 s4
rows: Compiled to MR / Tez / Spark jobs
Materialised to HDFS between every MapReduce stage
Vectorized execution (1,024-row batches), cost-based optimizer, connector architecture (HDFS, Hive, Cassandra, MySQL, Kafka, S3 in one query)
key: Hive compiles queries into batch MapReduce/Tez jobs that write intermediate results to HDFS (minutes), whereas Presto pipelines data through memory with no intermediate disk writes, giving second-level interactive SQL.
cue: If the question describes analysts needing sub-minute dashboard queries over petabytes on HDFS, the answer is Presto; a nightly multi-hour ETL is Hive.

key: Hive compiles HiveQL into batch jobs with minute-level latency, whereas Spark SQL optimises queries with Catalyst and runs them in memory in seconds, sharing Hive's Metastore.
cue: If the question wants SQL over the same Hive tables but with interactive latency plus streaming in one engine, the answer is Spark SQL.

slides: P1 s8, s29 (MCQ Q4 note), s32 (A2); P2 s12; W05 P2 s13
rows: Materialises intermediate data to HDFS between every MR stage
DAG-based successor to MapReduce (no per-job HDFS round trip)
Faster; Hive and Pig rewrote on Tez, reducing latency 5-10x
Same setting; Tez = 'DAG of tasks, faster'
LLAP (2016): Hive-on-Tez with persistent in-memory daemon, sub-second queries
key: Under MapReduce, Hive runs a chain of separate jobs that write intermediate results to HDFS, while Tez runs the same query as one DAG of tasks, cutting latency 5-10x with the same results.
cue: If the question asks how switching Hive's execution engine from MapReduce to Tez changes the plan for a top-5 query, the answer is: one DAG instead of chained MR jobs with HDFS writes between them.

slides: P1 s8, s10-11, s28 (MCQ Q1 note); P2 s7
rows: Table schemas, column types, partition info + HDFS path, SerDe, table statistics, privileges
Where data lives and how to parse it; partition pruning; cost-based optimizer stats
Cannot query any table even though data on HDFS is intact
De facto catalogue for Spark, Presto/Trino, Impala, Athena (AWS Glue)
key: The Hive Metastore is a relational DB holding table schemas, partitions and SerDe information, whereas the NameNode holds only HDFS block metadata; the NameNode is the common distractor for 'where is Hive schema stored'.
cue: If the question asks where Hive keeps column names, types and partition locations, the answer is the Metastore (MySQL/PostgreSQL), not the NameNode.

rows: Dataflow, more expressive than MR but still procedural
Programmers (general knowledge; slide only says Pig is procedural)
Hundreds of analysts who could write SQL but not Java - self-service access
key: Pig Latin is a procedural dataflow language, while HiveQL is declarative SQL that Hive compiles to MapReduce, letting SQL-only analysts query Hadoop without engineers.
cue: If the question asks which tool let non-programmer analysts query Hadoop with SQL, the answer is Hive; a step-by-step procedural dataflow script is Pig.

rows: Analyst writes SELECT, Hive writes the distributed job
Business analysts, data scientists, BI teams
Compiled into MapReduce jobs, Tez DAGs or Spark jobs
key: Java MapReduce needs 100+ lines and days per aggregation, whereas HiveQL lets analysts declare the query in SQL and Hive generates the distributed job ('Declare, don't program').
cue: If the question describes thousands of non-engineers needing to query petabytes, the answer is SQL-on-Hadoop (Hive) instead of Java MapReduce.

rows: Batch analytics; UPDATE only on ACID tables
key: OLTP systems handle many small real-time reads and writes on validated data with millisecond latency, while OLAP systems like Hive run large batch analytic scans over petabytes with minute-level latency.
cue: If the question describes the live bKash wallet database that must not be slowed down, it is OLTP (copy it out with Sqoop); the nightly analytics over HDFS is OLAP (Hive).

rows: Whole row groups inside a file
Min/max column stats in the file footer
WHERE on the partition column only
WHERE on any column with stats
year=2024 AND month=01 reads 1 sub-directory, not 36 months
score > 90: row group with [60,85] skipped; 10 TB may read only 50 GB
File level (then only the needed column chunk)
key: Partition pruning skips whole directories based on the partition-column value recorded in the Metastore, while predicate pushdown skips row groups within a columnar file using min/max statistics in the footer; the two stack.
cue: If the question filters on the partitioned date column, the saving is partition pruning; if it filters on an ordinary column inside Parquet files, it is predicate pushdown.

rows: SQL aggregation: GROUP BY song_a, song_b HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
Luigi task (declares output path + dependencies, skips finished outputs)
key: At Spotify, HiveQL did the one-pass SQL aggregation for features (playlist co-occurrence), while Spark did the iterative ALS model training, with Luigi chaining the two.
cue: If the question describes counting song pairs across billions of playlists, the answer is a HiveQL GROUP BY; training the recommendation model over many iterations is Spark.

rows: Each source publishes once to a central bus; consumers subscribe
New jobs, tightly bound to source
Zero changes to any source system
key: Point-to-point ETL wires every pair of systems directly (O(N^2) brittle nightly jobs, no replay), whereas an event-driven pipeline routes everything through one bus like Kafka, so sources and consumers are decoupled, real-time and replayable.
cue: If the question describes 50 systems with thousands of fragile nightly ETL jobs that break on every schema change, the answer is to replace them with a central Kafka event bus.

slides: P1 s7, s9-12; P1 s32 (MCQ Q1 note), s34 (T/F 1, 4)
rows: Logs -> HDFS: web server, application, IoT logs
Launches a MapReduce job; each map task reads a primary-key range; incremental import via last-value
Agent: Source -> Channel -> Sink; fan-in and fan-out
01:00 nightly: 10 M bKash rows Oracle -> HDFS Parquet
key: Sqoop bulk-copies relational database tables to and from HDFS with a parallel MapReduce job, while Flume continuously collects log files from many servers into HDFS through Source-Channel-Sink agents.
cue: If the question describes syncing 10 million customer records nightly from Oracle to Hadoop, the answer is Sqoop; collecting web-server access logs from many machines into HDFS is Flume.

rows: Optimised for log collection to HDFS
File channel survives agent crash; no replay (inference: slide credits Kafka with the stronger durability and replay)
Stronger durability and replay from any offset
Often replaced by Kafka producers writing directly from applications
Kafka Connect replaces Sqoop and Flume for most use cases
key: Flume is a specialised log-collection pipe into HDFS, whereas Kafka is a general-purpose durable event log that many consumers can read and replay, which is why Kafka has largely replaced Flume.
cue: If the question needs several independent consumers (fraud, balance, audit) to read the same events in real time and replay them, the answer is Kafka; just shipping server logs into HDFS is Flume.

rows: Retained for a configured period (days, weeks, or forever)
Reads from offset 0 and replays the entire history
Broker (inference from 'the Kafka broker never tracks what a consumer has read')
Consumer tracks its own offset; broker never tracks it
Each consumer (group) reads independently at its own offset
New pipelines built without re-ingesting from source
key: A traditional queue deletes a message once consumed and the broker tracks delivery, whereas Kafka keeps an append-only log for a retention period and each consumer tracks its own offset, so late or new consumers can replay history.
cue: If the question describes a new analytics team that needs last week's events without re-ingesting from the source database, the answer is Kafka's retained log (start at offset 0).

rows: Sustained 100 MB/s per broker, multi-day retention, replay
Transactional messaging: few thousand msgs/sec, guaranteed delivery, complex routing
Disk -> kernel -> user space -> socket -> NIC (4 copies)
Pull; one log serves all consumers
key: ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ were built for low-volume transactional messaging with per-message acknowledgements, whereas Kafka uses sequential append-only logs, zero-copy, batching and consumer pull to reach ~10x their throughput with retention and replay.
cue: If the question asks why LinkedIn could not use ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ for billions of activity events per day, the answer: they targeted a few thousand msgs/sec without retention or replay; Kafka reached 50.5 MB/s vs 4.3/14.7.

rows: Two (batch + stream) - must stay in sync
High: two systems, merging layer; 30-40% of effort keeping layers consistent
Very high (Spark/Hive on full dataset); HDFS master dataset
Limited by stream engine; Kafka (bounded) + S3/Iceberg
Logic too complex for stream-only; batch ML training; regulatory batch reports
Stream engine fast enough to reprocess; single code path worth the stream-storage cost
key: Lambda runs a batch layer and a speed layer with the same logic implemented twice and merges them in a serving layer, whereas Kappa drops the batch layer and uses one stream-processing code path, reprocessing history by replaying the Kafka log from offset 0.
cue: If the question describes a team tired of maintaining the same logic in Spark batch and Spark Streaming, the answer is Kappa; if a regulator mandates separate batch reconciliation or TB+ history is too slow to replay, keep Lambda.

slides: P1 s21-23, s33 (MCQ Q3 note); P2 s15-16
rows: Complete, immutable master dataset (HDFS); periodically recomputes batch views
New data arriving since the last batch job
Kafka -> S3 -> Spark + Iceberg, ~1 day (ML training, billing)
Kafka -> Flink, < 1 minute (dashboards, alerts, A/B counters)
Query = batch view (up to N hours ago)
key: The batch layer periodically recomputes accurate views from the full immutable master dataset (hours stale), while the speed layer processes only recent data with a stream engine to give approximate results within seconds; the serving layer merges the two.
cue: If the question asks which Lambda layer gives real-time low-latency views, the answer is the speed layer (not the serving layer, which only merges and serves).

rows: Schema-on-write: must fit the schema at load (W07 s13)
Raw data, any format: structured, semi-structured, unstructured; open files (Parquet, ORC, CSV, JSON, Avro)
Validated, structured tables (general knowledge; W07 s13: proprietary storage format)
Cheap and quick; transformation on demand
HDFS or S3/ADLS zones raw -> processed -> curated; Spark, Hive, Presto
Enterprise DW, e.g. Teradata, Oracle (1990s) (W07 P2 s4)
Data science, ML, exploration on raw history (general knowledge)
Fixed reports, BI dashboards on cleaned data (general knowledge)
Becomes a data swamp without governance
Rigid: schema must be defined upfront
key: A data lake stores raw data of any format cheaply and applies schema only when read, whereas a data warehouse validates data into a fixed schema before loading (schema-on-write), trading flexibility for clean, fast queries.
cue: If the question describes dumping raw logs, images and tables into S3/HDFS for later exploration, the answer is a data lake; cleaned, pre-defined tables for fixed business reports is a warehouse.

rows: Catalogue/governance layer (Apache Atlas, AWS Glue, Hive Metastore) tracks schemas, lineage, ownership, access
No catalogue: analysts cannot find relevant datasets
No one knows which files are current vs stale
Table format (Delta Lake, Iceberg) adds ACID
Multiple copies with different transformations, no version control
PII mixed with non-sensitive data, violating privacy regulations
Raw files accumulate without metadata, owners or quality guarantees
key: A data swamp is a data lake without governance, where raw files pile up with no catalogue, owners, versions or access control; enforcing a catalogue at ingest, owners, access control, quality checks and a table format keeps it a lake.
cue: If the question describes analysts unable to find datasets, unclear current files and PII mixed in, the answer is a data swamp - prevent it with a catalogue at ingest, owners, access control, automated checks, Delta/Iceberg.

rows: Speed matters and loss is tolerable
key: A memory channel buffers Flume events in RAM (fast but lost on restart), while a file channel persists them on disk so the buffer survives an agent crash.
cue: If the question says the Flume agent crashed and no log events may be lost, the answer is the file channel.

rows: Never updates in place; append-only writes; OS page cache prefetches next pages
Near-disk-bandwidth on spinning disk without SSD
key: Kafka only ever appends to the end of a log, so disk access is sequential (~600 MB/s on HDD) instead of random, which is a core reason it runs fast on spinning disks.
cue: If the question asks why Kafka is fast without SSDs, the answer starts with sequential append-only writes (plus zero-copy, batching, partition parallelism). Note: the two decks give the random-I/O figure as <1 MB/s (P1) and ~100 MB/s (P2) - quote the slide you cite.

rows: Disk -> kernel buffer -> user space -> socket buffer -> NIC
Disk -> kernel buffer -> NIC via Linux sendfile()
key: A traditional broker copies each message through user space (4 copies), while Kafka's sendfile() moves data from the kernel page cache straight to the network card (2 copies), doubling throughput with near-zero CPU.
cue: If the question asks what zero-copy means in Kafka, the answer: sendfile() skips the user-space copy, so 4 copies become 2.

rows: Two separate ingestion paths -> data inconsistency
All events written to Kafka first; speed and batch layers are both consumers of the same topic
7-day Kafka retention lets them replay any window when a Flink/Spark job has a bug
Flink (<1 min), S3 + Spark + Iceberg (~1 day), Cassandra + Druid serving
Increasingly moved batch jobs to Flink (Kappa simplification)
Kafka's durable log absorbs 5x Super Bowl spikes; Flink catches up
key: Netflix removed classic Lambda's dual-ingestion problem by writing every event to Kafka first so both layers read the same durable log, and gradually shifted batch work to Flink streams (towards Kappa).
cue: If the question asks how to keep Lambda's batch and speed layers consistent, the answer is Netflix's pattern: one Kafka topic as the single source of truth feeding both layers.

rows: Ordered append-only log, one of P splits of a topic, stored on a broker (leader + R-1 replicas)
HDFS sub-directory per value of the partition column
Parallelism: P producers and up to P consumers in a group; key-level ordering
Producer: key hash or round-robin (same key -> same partition)
Throughput scales linearly with partition count
High-cardinality key -> millions of directories crash NameNode
Spark partition = slice of an RDD processed in parallel by one task on an executor
key: A Kafka partition is an ordered log segment of a topic that gives parallelism and per-key ordering, while a Hive partition is a directory per column value that lets queries skip data; same word, different jobs.
cue: If the question is about consumer parallelism or keeping one driver's GPS pings in order, it means Kafka partitions; if about skipping data in a WHERE clause, it means Hive partitions.

rows: Ink that does not convey data
Decorative borders, 3-D effects, gradient fills, redundant legends, heavy gridlines, vibrations, ducks
If erasing does not reduce information, erase it
Raises data-ink ratio = data ink / total ink
Lowers the ratio; 3-D distorts quantitative comparison
One thick bar encoding one value can have a high ratio
Ratio is about what ink encodes, not how much (not printing cost)
key: Data-ink is ink that encodes actual values, while chartjunk is decoration that encodes nothing; Tufte says to maximise the share of data-ink by erasing anything whose removal loses no information.
cue: If the question describes a bar chart with 3-D shading, gradient fills, heavy gridlines and a one-series legend, those are chartjunk - remove them to raise the data-ink ratio.

rows: Same chart structure repeated across subsets (districts, years) in a grid; trellis/facet chart
Word-sized data graphics embedded in text or table cells
Same axis scale in every panel so magnitudes are comparable
Trend shape only, no separate figure
Temporal context next to a number
District daily case count with an inline trend
Tableau Pages shelf; ggplot2 facet_wrap / facet_grid
Grafana stat panel; Bloomberg terminal; GitHub contribution heatmap
key: Small multiples repeat the same full chart, on the same scale, for each subset so subsets can be compared side by side, whereas a sparkline is a tiny word-sized trend line placed inline next to a number.
cue: If the question wants to compare the trend of 50 states or 8 divisions at once, the answer is small multiples; if it wants a trend beside each number in a table, sparklines.

rows: Forces the viewer to remember the previous frame
Animated map of spreading cases was less actionable
12 monthly temperature charts in a 3 x 4 grid
key: Small multiples show every subset at once so the eye can compare directly, whereas animation shows one frame at a time and makes the viewer remember earlier frames, so small multiples beat animation.
cue: If the question asks whether to animate a spreading-disease map or show a grid of state charts, the answer is the small-multiples grid (NYT lesson).

rows: Each point drawn at low opacity (alpha = 0.02); dense regions look darker
2-D area split into hexagonal grid; count points per hex; colour by count
Count per area; 10 M points -> ~10,000 hex cells
Still fails at very high densities
Individual points inside a cell are hidden (general knowledge)
key: Alpha transparency keeps every point but makes each faint so density shows as darkness (and saturates at extreme density), while hexbin replaces points with hexagon counts, which scales to millions of points.
cue: If the question has a 10-million-point scatter that is a solid blob and wants an interactive chart with counts, the answer is hexbin; a quick fix for moderate density is alpha.

rows: Grid of hexagons coloured by count
Contour lines or filled contours at probability levels
Estimates the continuous probability density of the point cloud
key: Hexbin counts points into discrete hexagonal cells, while KDE estimates a smooth continuous density and draws contours, revealing the shape, modes and tails of the cloud.
cue: If the question asks which overplotting fix best shows the shape and number of peaks (modes) of a distribution, the answer is KDE contours; for counts per area, hexbin.

rows: Materialise aggregate tables at all dimension combinations (district x date x product x channel) in advance
Return a statistically correct estimate by sampling the table
Pre-computed cube (millions of rows), not 100 B-row fact table
Staleness (up to 24 h; nightly Spark/Hive pre-agg job)
key: A data cube pre-computes exact aggregates in advance so dashboards answer in under a second but can be up to a day stale, whereas AQP samples the live table to give approximate answers in milliseconds.
cue: If the question describes a Tableau filter over 100 billion Hive rows that must respond in < 1 s and yesterday's numbers are fine, the answer is a data cube; if a fast approximate answer is acceptable, AQP - but never AQP for financial reconciliation.

slides: P1 s20, s22, s27 (MCQ Q4 note)
rows: Grafana polls the TSDB on a schedule
Server pushes updates via WebSocket; browser chart re-renders on each push
Ops dashboards: live driver count every 5 s, server metrics
key: Grafana pulls fresh data from the time-series database every few seconds, while a WebSocket + D3 setup has the server push each new value so the chart updates sub-second.
cue: If the question needs second-level ops monitoring with little coding, the answer is Grafana polling; if it needs sub-second live updates like an election needle, WebSocket push to D3.js.

slides: P1 s22-23, s27 (MCQ Q4); W08 P2 s22 (preview)
key: Tableau is drag-and-drop business BI with only limited scheduled refresh, whereas Grafana is built for real-time operational metrics, polling time-series databases every few seconds.
cue: If the question describes monitoring server metrics and error rates with a 5-second refresh, the answer is Grafana; quarterly business dashboards for managers, Tableau (or Power BI).

rows: Code: binds data to DOM (SVG) elements
Interactive SVG in the browser, not static PNG/PDF
NYT graphics, election needle; invented by Mike Bostock at NYT
key: Tableau and Power BI are drag-and-drop tools for business users, whereas D3.js is a code library that binds data to SVG elements for fully custom interactive web graphics.
cue: If the audience is business users, choose Tableau/Power BI; if a newsroom needs a custom interactive chart on the web, choose D3.js.

rows: <= 4 categories and the question is 'what fraction of the whole?'
Any comparison; > 5 categories (horizontal bar ordered by value)
Humans judge angles and arc lengths poorly
Avoid (pie listed under Avoid for temporal)
Line or bar chart always more readable
Grouped bar for comparison across groups
key: A pie chart only works for a few (<= 4) parts of a whole because people judge angles poorly, while a bar chart uses length, which people read accurately, so it wins for comparisons, many categories and time.
cue: If the question shows a pie chart comparing 8 product categories or months, the answer is to replace it with a (horizontal) bar chart, or a line chart for time.

key: A choropleth colours regions to show a rate or proportion, while a proportional bubble map scales circles to show absolute counts.
cue: If the question wants dengue incidence per 100,000 by district, the answer is a choropleth; total case numbers by city, a bubble map.

rows: What is the spread and shape of X?
What is the spread of X, where are the outliers?
key: A histogram shows the full shape of a distribution, while a box plot summarises it by quartiles and flags outliers (a violin adds density to the quartiles).
cue: If the question asks for the chart showing distribution and spread of a continuous variable, the answer is a histogram; to highlight quartiles and outliers, a box plot.

rows: Identical: mean x 9.0, mean y 7.5, var x 11.0, r 0.816, y = 3 + 0.5x
Four different stories: linear, curved, outlier, vertical cluster
Opposite trends in sub-populations average out; means meaningless on log-scale data
First and most powerful quality check
Daily average hides sudden regime changes
DGHS monthly averages look stable year-over-year
Line chart reveals June-Aug cholera and October dengue peaks
key: Summary statistics can be identical for very different data (Anscombe's Quartet), while a plot reveals the actual pattern, so visualise before trusting the numbers - more so at big-data scale.
cue: If the question says annual averages look stable but asks what is being missed, the answer is to plot the time series (seasonal spikes hidden by the mean, Anscombe's lesson).

rows: The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (book, self-published)
The Eyes Have It (IEEE Visual Languages paper)
What to show and what to remove (static design)
How users interact: overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand
Data-ink ratio, chartjunk, lie factor, small multiples, sparklines
Mantra, seven data types, seven tasks, treemap (1991), dynamic queries
Tableau 'Remove formatting', Grafana minimal theme, D3 no default axes
Tableau drill-down, Grafana time-range zoom, Google Maps zoom
National total first; state dropdown; hover tooltip
key: Tufte tells you what ink belongs on a chart (maximise data-ink, remove chartjunk, avoid lies), while Shneiderman tells you how an interactive visualisation should behave (overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand).
cue: If the question is about removing 3-D effects or gridlines, cite Tufte; if it is about a dashboard's drill-down flow or tooltips, cite Shneiderman's mantra.

rows: NYT's choice: a data quality decision encoded in the visual design
Choosing 7 vs 14 changes the story - editorial decision with ethical weight
key: Both smooth out the weekly reporting cycle, but a 7-day average reacts faster to real changes while a 14-day average is smoother and lags more; the choice changes the story the chart tells.
cue: If the question asks why NYT used a 7-day average, the answer is to remove day-of-week reporting artefacts while staying responsive; the slide's point is that the window choice is an editorial decision.

slides: P1 s9-10, s31 (MCQ Q2 note); P2 s11
rows: Which community/group is a node in?
Start each node alone; greedily merge to maximise modularity; aggregate super-nodes; stop when gain is zero
O(n log n); billion-node graphs in Spark GraphX
K-Means clusters vectors, not graph topologies
key: Louvain finds groups of densely connected nodes by maximising modularity, whereas PageRank scores how important each individual node is; K-Means clusters feature vectors, not graphs.
cue: If the question asks to find political factions or coordinated bot networks in a follower graph, the answer is Louvain; to rank the most influential accounts, PageRank.

rows: Only 22.1% mutual; 77.9% of users have a non-reciprocating follower
News medium: 85% of trending topics were headline news
Retweet cascades wide and shallow (one hop from a celebrity)
Power-law in-degree alpha ~2.276; average path 4.12 hops
key: Twitter is a directed, mostly non-reciprocal follower graph (22.1% mutual) that behaves like a news medium, while Facebook is a mutual-friendship social network (~100% reciprocal).
cue: If the question describes one-to-many broadcasting where a celebrity's post spreads widely in one hop, the answer is Twitter as a news medium; mutual friendship ties spreading along long chains is Facebook.

rows: Which nodes form a densely connected group?
Which k nodes to seed so information spreads to the most users?
Kempe et al. (KDD 2003 Best Paper): NP-hard, greedy approximation with (1 - 1/e) guarantee
Interest groups, political factions, professional clusters, bot networks
Seed users for a product promotion or message
Profiling group membership (general knowledge; D1 asks for one)
Manipulation / microtargeting vulnerable users (slide s12 mentions microtargeting)
key: Community detection groups nodes that are densely linked to each other, whereas influence maximisation chooses a small set of seed nodes that will spread information furthest (NP-hard, greedy (1 - 1/e) approximation).
cue: If the question describes a marketer choosing 50 accounts to start a campaign, the answer is influence maximisation; finding coordinated bot clusters is community detection.

rows: Classical statistical: AR(p) past values, I(d) differencing, MA(q) past errors
Additive decomposable model y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + e(t)
Fourier series; multiple seasonalities (annual, weekly, daily)
h(t): user-specified events (Eid, Puja, elections, cricket World Cup)
Expert parameter selection (p, d, q); cannot hand-fit 10,000 series
Analysts, not statisticians; interpretable parameters; robust to missing data/outliers
Short stationary series, no strong seasonality, small datasets
Thousands of business series; one Spark partition per series via applyInPandas
key: ARIMA is a classical model that needs a stationary series and expert-chosen (p, d, q), while Prophet decomposes a series into trend, multiple seasonalities and holidays with automatic changepoints, so analysts can fit thousands of series at scale.
cue: If the question describes 5,000 SKUs with weekly and yearly seasonality and Eid spikes, the answer is Prophet; a short, stationary series with no strong seasonality can use ARIMA.

rows: g + s + h structure lets epidemiologists inspect each component
Domain experts can audit and adjust each component (holidays, trend flexibility)
Also in the ensemble (Prophet, ARIMA, LSTM, human experts); no single model wins every season
key: Prophet's additive trend + seasonality + holiday components can be inspected and adjusted by domain experts, while black-box deep learning forecasters like LSTM cannot, which is why the slides credit Prophet's trust in public health.
cue: If the question asks why epidemiologists trusted Prophet over a deep-learning forecaster, the answer is decomposability/interpretability; if asked which single model is best, the answer is none - ensembles win.

rows: Ensemble of random trees isolating points by partitioning feature space
Residual whose |value| > k x IQR of residuals
Fewer splits to isolate -> shorter path length
Scales to millions of observations in Spark MLlib
bKash agent: 10 -> 10,000 transactions/hour flagged as possible money laundering
key: STL flags points whose residual after removing trend and seasonality is unusually large, which is interpretable but needs regular seasonality, whereas Isolation Forest flags points that random trees isolate in few splits, with no distribution assumption and Spark-scale speed.
cue: If the question describes millions of mobile agents with no clear seasonal pattern (bKash money laundering), the answer is Isolation Forest; a single seasonal series where you must explain the alert, STL.

rows: Fit 5,000 Prophet models one after another
Group by sku_id; applyInPandas sends each SKU to one partition; Prophet in a Pandas UDF
Written to Hive/S3 as Parquet, served to dashboard
Prophet on 60 HHS regions simultaneously via applyInPandas
key: Fitting thousands of independent forecasts one by one takes hours, but because each series is independent Spark can group by series and run Prophet in parallel with applyInPandas (8 h -> ~12 min).
cue: If the question asks how to parallelise 5,000 store-product forecasts, the answer is groupBy(sku_id).applyInPandas(prophet_fit), one series per partition.

rows: Order matters: shuffling rows destroys the signal; timestamps must be kept
Seasonality, trend must be modelled explicitly
Mean/variance may change; most models need differencing
key: Time series observations are ordered and autocorrelated with trend and seasonality, so shuffling them destroys the signal, whereas i.i.d. tabular rows are independent and order-free.
cue: If a True/False says shuffling a time series does not change the analysis, it is False; standard regression is invalid because of autocorrelation.

rows: >3,000 sentinel physicians report weekly ILI counts
Social media, pharmacy OTC sales, ER chief complaints, search query volume
Twitter peaks 7-10 days before ER visits; pharmacy 3-5 days before confirmation
Clinic -> state health dept -> CDC weekly report
Kafka -> Spark Streaming (NLP + aggregation) -> alert engine -> Grafana
key: Traditional surveillance counts physician-reported cases (accurate but 1-2 weeks late), while syndromic surveillance watches non-clinical signals such as tweets, pharmacy sales and searches for earlier but noisier warnings - a supplement, not a replacement.
cue: If the question describes detecting a flu or dengue outbreak days before hospitals report it, the answer is syndromic surveillance - validated against ILINet/DGHS ground truth.

rows: Real-time ED data from 3,500+ emergency departments (38 M visits in 2019-20)
r² = 0.97 on 2003-08, then over-predicted flu 2x in 2012-13; discontinued
Primary signal in post-GFT Prophet nowcasting
Big data hubris; algorithm confounding (autocomplete changes); media amplification
Exogenous covariate (e.g. Twitter), not a replacement
key: Google Flu Trends used search queries as a proxy for flu and failed (2x over-prediction) because searches track anxiety and media, while BioSense uses direct emergency-department observations as the primary signal, adding proxies only as covariates.
cue: If the question asks why Google Flu Trends failed, the answer: a proxy signal with hubris, autocomplete confounding and media amplification; the fix is direct ED data with proxies as covariates.

rows: Healthcare data: patient records, medical information
De-identify 18 PHI identifiers before research use; consent required
Data minimisation; purpose limitation; right to erasure
PDPA: under development, based on GDPR principles; NID-linked records require explicit consent
Not financial data (that is GLBA / Basel III)
key: HIPAA is the US healthcare-specific law requiring removal of 18 identifiers before research use, while GDPR is the EU's general data-protection law built on data minimisation, purpose limitation and the right to erasure; Bangladesh's PDPA is being modelled on GDPR.
cue: If the question mentions removing 18 identifiers from US patient records, the answer is HIPAA; a user demanding their data be deleted, GDPR's right to erasure; NID-linked consent in Bangladesh, PDPA.

rows: Statistical disclosure analysis by a qualified expert
Name, DOB, zip, NID, phone, etc.
HIPAA de-identification method (general knowledge; slide lists it only as a technique)
key: Safe harbour de-identifies by deleting a fixed list of 18 identifiers, while expert determination relies on a qualified expert's statistical analysis that re-identification risk is acceptable.
cue: If the question says 'remove name, DOB, zip, NID and phone before sharing', the answer is safe harbour; 'a statistician certifies the risk is low', expert determination.

rows: Adds calibrated noise to aggregate statistics
Trains models at each hospital without moving raw data
Inferring an individual record from statistics
Model updates move; raw records stay
key: Differential privacy protects individuals by adding calibrated noise to released aggregates, whereas federated learning protects them by keeping raw data at each hospital and training the model where the data lives.
cue: If the question says hospitals cannot share patient records but want one joint model, the answer is federated learning; publishing district counts so nobody can be singled out, differential privacy.

rows: Diagnoses (ICD-10), medications, labs, vital signs, clinical notes
Structured, plus semi-structured HL7 FHIR and free-text notes
Unstructured binary files (200 MB - 2 GB each)
ML: random forest (ICU mortality AUROC > 0.90), gradient boosting (readmission)
Being stored in files does not make it structured (T/F 4 False)
key: EHR data is mostly structured clinical fields (diagnoses, labs, vitals) suited to tabular ML, whereas DICOM images are large unstructured binary files analysed with deep learning, not SQL.
cue: If the question asks how to classify MRI/CT scans, the answer is unstructured data, analysed with CNNs; ICU mortality from vitals and labs uses structured EHR with random forest.

rows: Evoformer transformer on multiple sequence alignments (MSAs)
Months per protein, thousands of dollars
170,000 solved structures in the Protein Data Bank (training set)
MSA search over UniProt's 250 M sequences; 128 TPU v3 cores for weeks
Median GDT > 92%; 200 M predicted structures released (2022)
key: Experimental methods like X-ray crystallography take months per protein, while AlphaFold predicts the 3-D structure from sequence alone by learning from 170,000 solved structures and alignments over 250 million sequences.
cue: If the question asks what AlphaFold solved and why it is big data, the answer: protein structure prediction from sequence, using MSAs over 250 M UniProt sequences.
